newsitem.title: FRANCE: Algeria passes election law setting dual parliament.
newsitem.headline: Algeria passes election law setting dual parliament.

text.p: Algeria's government-appointed Transitional National Council (CNT) on Sunday voted an election law setting up a 524-seat, parliament of two houses, Algerian state-run radio said.

The CNT, a unelected quasi-parliament, passed the law at the end of a special voting session called by President Liamine Zeroual to set in place the legal framework for his plan to hold elections which the authorities see as a way of ending five years of crisis and violence with Islamist groups.
Algeria has been without an elected parliament since January 1992 when the authorities scrapped a general election dominated by Islamic fundamentalists.
The law passed on Sunday states the number of seats for the upper house would be 380, including eight for deputies elected by Algerian expatriates, the radio said.
The law broadly sets one seat for 80,000 inhabitants with a minium of four seats for each province.
Algiers emerged as the constituency with the most seats -- a total of 24 -- while some sparsely populated southern provinces have four seats, the law stipulates.
Under the Algerian constitution, adopted last November, the National Assembly and the National Council (upper house) will form the new parliament.

Two thirds of the National Council's 144 members will be designated by elected local authorities while the other third will be picked by the president from the ranks of leading personalities, union officials and senior state servants.
Scrapping the last elections plunged Algeria's 29 million people into conflict which has lasted for five years and in which about 60,000 people have died.

Late last month, the CNT passed into law a voting system of proportional representation, replacing a straight majority poll under which the Islamic Salvation Front (FIS) had taken an overwhelming lead the previous general election.
President Liamine Zeroual's government has barred the outlawed FIS from fielding candidates in the upcoming elections but two legal fundamentalist groups, Hamas and Nahda, would compete in the poll.

Hamas, whose leader Mahfoud Nahnah gained one-third of the vote in the 1995 presidential election, is expected by Algerian commentators to play an important part in the elections planned to be held between May 29 and June 5.
